title: Operating Margin
subtitle: Measuring operating efficiency after indirect costs too
openingOptions: For every 100 dong of revenue, 15 dong is operating profit
The company earns 15% in net profit after all tax has been paid
explanation: Operating margin divides EBIT by revenue, measuring what remains after both cost of goods sold and operating costs like selling, admin, and R&D. Because it subtracts more, it is always lower than gross margin. The gap between the two margins is the most valuable piece of information: it shows how much of every dong of gross profit the operating machine is consuming, and that gap widening over time is a sign costs are getting out of control.

diagram.label: Subtract selling, admin, and R&D costs
The gap between the two margins shows how costly operations are

realWorldExample.description: Microsoft's Operating Margin usually exceeds 40% thanks to software economics: once development is done, producing one more copy costs almost nothing (extremely low marginal cost), letting operating profit scale much faster than revenue as the company grows.

quiz.question: Which type of business usually has the highest Operating Margin?
options: Airlines - because ticket prices are high and the marginal cost per passenger is very low
Supermarkets - because fast inventory turnover accumulates high profit
Construction - because large contracts mean high profit per project
Software/SaaS - marginal cost near zero as it scales
quiz.explanation: Software/SaaS has very high operating margin (often 20-40%+) because the cost of serving one more customer is close to zero. Transportation, retail, and construction, by contrast, run on thin margins.

quiz.question: Why is the gap between a company's Gross Margin and Operating Margin valuable information worth tracking?
options: A large gap = operating costs are consuming a lot of gross profit
This gap carries no meaningful analytical signal at all
You only need to look at Operating Margin, Gross Margin doesn't matter
The gap is fixed for every company, so there's no need to track it
quiz.explanation: Tracking both margins together gives a fuller picture: Gross Margin shows production/purchasing efficiency, while the gap to Operating Margin shows whether the company is controlling selling and admin costs effectively.

quiz.question: Revenue is 1,500 billion, EBIT is 180 billion. What is the Operating Margin?
options: 8.3x (= 1,500 ÷ 180, numerator and denominator swapped)
12% (= 180 ÷ 1,500, EBIT over revenue)
18% (= 180 ÷ 1,000, revenue rounded down)
1,320 billion (= 1,500 − 180, taking the difference instead of the ratio)
quiz.explanation: Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue = 180/1,500 = 12%. This is what remains after both cost of goods sold and operating costs, but before interest and tax - so it measures core business efficiency.

quiz.question: Gross Margin stays stable but Operating Margin keeps falling over three years. Where does the problem lie?
options: In raw-material input prices rising faster than selling prices
In selling and administrative costs, not cost of goods sold
In rising interest expense as the business takes on new debt
In an increase to the corporate tax rate during the period
quiz.explanation: These two margins differ only in the block of operating costs. If cost of goods stays proportionally the same while operating margin keeps falling, that means SG&A is growing faster than revenue.

quiz.question: Operating Margin is negative but Gross Margin is still a positive 40%. What does that mean?
options: The business recorded a large foreign-exchange loss at year end
The business is selling below its own cost of goods sold just to grab market share from rivals
Interest expense has exceeded gross profit during the period
Sales are profitable at the gross level but operating costs swallow it all
quiz.explanation: Interest expense doesn't yet sit inside Operating Margin, so the culprit can only be SG&A. This is the familiar picture of a cash-burning startup: the product has decent margins, but the headcount and marketing machine outgrew today's revenue base.

keyTakeaways: Measures operating efficiency after SG&A and R&D
Software/SaaS has the highest operating margin thanks to scalability

practicePrompt.question: A company has Revenue = 1,000 billion, Gross Profit = 400 billion, and after subtracting SG&A + R&D, EBIT = 150 billion remains. What is this company's Operating Margin?
options: Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue = 150/1,000 = 15%, so 15 dong of operating profit per 100 dong of revenue
Operating Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue = 400/1,000 = 40%, since this is exactly the formula for Operating Margin
Operating Margin = EBIT / Gross Profit = 150/400 = 37.5%, since EBIT must be compared against gross profit rather than revenue
Operating Margin has no meaning once a company already has Gross Margin to assess business efficiency
practicePrompt.explanation: Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue = 150/1,000 = 15%. This measures whole-business operating efficiency (after subtracting both production cost and selling/admin costs), unlike Gross Margin which only measures production efficiency.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Measures operating efficiency after SG&A and R&D

application.title: Calculate Operating Margin
application.message: From an income statement you already have Gross Profit; subtract SG&A and R&D to get EBIT, then divide by Revenue for Operating Margin - compare it against the Gross Margin you just calculated in the previous lesson.
application.secondary: The gap between these two margins tells you how much the company spends on running operations.

sections.text: Gross Margin only subtracts direct production costs. Operating Margin goes one step further: it also subtracts selling and general administrative costs (SG&A) and research and development (R&D) - showing how efficiently a business actually operates, not just how well it produces.

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue (EBIT = earnings before interest and tax)
Operating Margin is always lower than Gross Margin

This is a mathematical rule, not an anomaly: since EBIT = Gross Profit − SG&A − R&D, Operating Margin can never exceed Gross Margin. What matters is how large that gap is, and whether it is widening or narrowing over the years.
Why Microsoft has an Operating Margin above 40%

Software has very particular economics: once the initial development cost is spent, producing one more copy costs almost nothing extra (near-zero marginal cost). As revenue rises, most of that increase falls straight through to operating profit instead of being 'eaten' by proportionally rising production costs - this is why SaaS/software companies have Operating Margins far above manufacturing, retail, or airlines.

items: Software/SaaS: Operating Margin usually 20-40%+ thanks to near-zero marginal cost
Retail, construction, airlines: Operating Margin often just a few percent due to heavy operating costs
A widening Gross Margin − Operating Margin gap = SG&A/R&D is growing faster than revenue
A narrowing gap over time = the company is controlling operating costs better as it scales

lines: Tracking Gross Margin and Operating Margin side by side gives a much fuller picture than looking at either one alone.

example.title: Separating the trading from the financing
example.calculation: Revenue VND 2,000bn · cost of sales 1,300bn · selling and admin 400bn → EBIT 300bn · interest 120bn
example.result: Operating margin = 300 ÷ 2,000 = 15% · net margin after interest and 20% tax ≈ 7.2%
example.explanation: One business, two very different figures, and almost the whole gap from 15% to 7.2% is the VND 120bn of interest. Operating margin measures the trading; net margin measures the trading PLUS the financing. Pay down debt and the second number rises while the first does not move.
